Memory.value: My memories of the event come in disconnected pieces that do not fit together
When I have memories of what happened I sometimes hear things in my head that I heard during the frightening event.
My memories of the frightening event are like a film that plays over and over.

vignette: Four years ago, Tariq’s younger brother collapsed onto the floor of a downtown city bus after working a seventy-two-hour stretch at the hospital. In the sudden violence of the man who struck him, Sami’s coat had torn open, leaving him naked and defenseless against the grimy floorboards as he lay unresponsive. Tariq had arrived at the next stop, found his brother’s scattered belongings, and watched paramedics work under the harsh glare of emergency lights. The memory of that afternoon never settled into a single story. Instead, it arrived in disconnected pieces that refused to align: the scuff of a sneaker on linoleum, the sharp hiss of an oxygen mask sealing shut, the way Sami’s hand had fallen limp against a metal pole. When the pieces surfaced, they brought with them the exact pitch of the bus’s air brakes and the rhythmic thump of a medevac radio against a dashboard. Tariq had come to believe that those moments were not finished; they played over and over in his mind like a film reel he could not pause, the images flickering through his thoughts during the quiet hours of the night. What frightened him most was the conviction that danger operated just beneath the surface of everyday spaces. He developed a habit of cataloguing potential weapons or dangerous objects in any environment he entered: letter openers left on conference desks, heavy glass door handles, the glint of a maintenance wrench in a supply closet. He studied the faces and body language of people he passed, reading for tension in jawlines or shifts in posture that might signal an approaching threat. He also found himself avoiding going to unfamiliar places because he could not assess the danger until he had mapped the exits. These habits of scanning and avoidance settled into his daily routine. His publisher office sat on the eighth floor of a glass-fronted building, but the daily grind required him to traverse uncarpeted loading docks and navigate the sprawling, multi-wing editing suites where layout tables were arranged without clear signage. He began declining trips to those scattered neighborhoods, opting instead to conduct all editorial reviews from his familiar desk. The fifteen-minute ride to the bus stop at 6:45 a.m. became the day’s first hurdle. The moment the doors hissed open, his chest tightened; the specific architecture of the seats, the sway of the vehicle, and the sudden stops all pulled him back to the exact conditions of Sami’s collapse. He learned to endure the journey by gripping the overhead rail until his knuckles ached, treating the transit as an obstacle to be survived rather than a passage. At work, Tariq also found that feeling very tired or exhausted no longer felt like a simple lack of rest. When fatigue set in, his mind would fracture the way it had during those weeks following the incident. He had come to believe that exhaustion was a prelude to losing control, so he began scheduling his editing deadlines around strict rest cycles, leaving several manuscript submissions unreviewed. The film-like quality of his recollections meant that during quiet moments in his editor’s office, the sequence would begin without warning—the squeal of the bus brakes, the crack of the initial impact, the startled gasp of a fellow passenger—and he would have to steady himself against the edge of his mahogany desk until the sequence completed itself. His publisher colleagues noted his reliability had not changed, but his routes had grown rigid, his willingness to explore new editing suites or regional author properties had steadily narrowed. Over the past eight months, these patterns had calcified. His marriage, once built on spontaneous dinners and weekend trips, now revolved around carefully mapped routines. He avoided unfamiliar places so thoroughly that his wife began planning their weekends entirely within their home neighborhood. He did not want to burden her with the logistics of staying close to home, but the weight of maintaining constant readiness had begun to fray his evenings. What finally brought him to his therapist’s office was not a single breakdown, but the quiet realization that he was no longer reading manuscripts with the same clarity. He had come to believe that his mind was stuck in a loop that threatened to spill into his work and his marriage, and what he hoped for was simply to find a way to stop waiting for the next bus, the next stranger’s glance, the next moment of exhaustion to turn into dread. He wanted to sit in a room and speak of what happened without feeling as though he were already bracing for it.
